Why do scuba divers enter the water by falling backwards from a sitting position? Why not a cannonball or pencil dive?
To make sure their equipment stay in place, breathing thingy in the mouth and air tanks.

I'm not a diver, but I've been told that doing something like a pencil dive would make them go too deep too fast. I believe they need to set up some stuff on their equipment once they are in the water before they start actually diving.

As far as going in backwards, I think it's mainly because all that stuff is pretty heavy above water and going in backwards is easier than doing a belly flop.

Hopefully some real divers can provide more info.

It is true you don't want to sink too fast but the main reason is that you want all your gear to stay on and in place. Usually your boyancy control device (BCD vest) is partially inflated when you get into the water and when you hit the water that can pull up and get you all tangled.

The back roll, forward roll, or step are all ways to enter the water without upsetting your gear. Usually the vest you wear to control buoyancy is partially inflated so you float and can dive at a controlled rate. With the vest inflated, hitting the water can pull that up off of the body and mess up the arrangement of all of your gear. Entering the water in a way that is controlled helps keep things orderly and comfortable.
Some even throw their gear in so it floats on the water and jump in after. They then put on all the gear in the water.

In addition to keeping the gear in place, it lessens the distance your upper body falls, and keeps your head away from the boat/ramp/whatever to ensure you don't end up with a concussion.

Edited to add: Also, going forward on land with those flippers on is awkward at best, disastrous at worst.
